note: Organises mitigation into eleven method areas and lists open source libraries, which is practical for recommending remediation.
title: Fairness in Machine Learning: A Survey

reading.body:
Fairness mitigation in machine learning is organized by when it acts, before, during, or after training, across eleven method areas, with open source libraries listed for each.

The survey's contribution is a map rather than a method. It sorts remedies by the stage at which they intervene, which matters because the choice of stage determines what a team can change and what it must accept. Pre-training fixes alter data or labels, in-training fixes alter the objective, and post-training fixes alter outputs. The eleven areas are the field's working taxonomy, and the listed libraries are what a practitioner can actually install.

The coverage extends past binary classification to regression, recommender systems, and unsupervised learning. That matters for AI systems generally, because most deployed models are not yes or no classifiers, and fairness work that assumes they are will not transfer. The survey also names five unresolved tensions, which is a statement that the field has not converged on a single correct approach.

What this does not provide is any measurement. There are no benchmarks, no datasets, no error rates, and no comparison of methods against each other. The citation count of 945 indicates the survey is widely referenced, but the data here says nothing about compute, data centers, or power, and no claim about those should be drawn from it. It is a 2020 survey of a methods literature, and its usefulness is as an index, not as evidence about how any particular system behaves.

explain_beginner: This survey explains that machine learning can affect people in important ways, so companies and researchers must watch for unfair outcomes linked to gender, ethnicity, or disability. The fairness literature is large and difficult for newcomers, so the authors map the main ideas and remedies. They group fixes by when they happen, before training, during training, and after training, then split these into eleven areas. They also cover fairness beyond simple yes or no predictions, including regression, recommender systems, and unsupervised learning, and point to publicly available software tools. It matters because it gives a practical starting point for reducing bias.
explain_business: This survey says that when machine learning affects people, leaders need confidence that it will not create unexpected social harm, such as bias related to gender, ethnicity, or disability. The fairness field is complex, so the authors provide a structured overview. They group remedies by when they are applied, before training, during training, and after training, with eleven method areas. They also cover settings beyond yes or no prediction and list publicly available software libraries. In practice, this helps executives decide how to assess and remediate fairness risks, where to look for tools, and why unresolved tensions require ongoing governance rather than a single fix.
explain_practitioner: This survey reviews fairness approaches for machine learning. It organizes mitigation methods by the stage at which they act, before training, during training, and after training. Within that structure, it identifies eleven method areas. The authors note that most published work focuses on yes or no prediction, but they also discuss fairness for regression, recommender systems, and unsupervised learning. They list publicly available software libraries. The key result is a practical map of the field, plus five unresolved tensions that summarize open fairness challenges. This helps researchers choose remediation strategies and locate tools, while seeing where evidence remains limited.
